meta.title: Who really said "send a barrel of this whiskey to every general in the army"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lincoln denied saying it — and identified the original himself: an older story about King George and General Wolfe. The anecdote first appears anonymously in the New York Herald, 18 September 1863.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'send a barrel of this whiskey to every general in the army'?
meta.ogDescription: Lincoln was asked directly and denied it, saying it 'would be very good if he had said it, but he did not' — then named the older King George story it came from.

answer.label: Not Lincoln — he denied it, and named the original
answer.sourceLine: The story — a delegation demands Grant’s removal as a drunkard, and Lincoln asks what brand he drinks so he can send a barrel to the rest — first appears as an anonymous press anecdote in the New York Herald of 18 September 1863. Lincoln was asked about it directly and denied it, saying it would be very good if he had said it, but he did not, and supposing it was charged to him “to give it currency.” He then named the original: an older story about King George and General Wolfe.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Recorded by Maj. Thomas T. Eckert; published 1882
King George on General Wolfe: ‘I wish he would bite some of my other Generals’

source.excerpt: It would be very good if he had said it, but he did not.
trail: The anecdote’s first known printing is the New York Herald, 18 September 1863 — unsigned, unsourced, and attributed to no witness Quote Investigator ↗.

Major Thomas T. Eckert, who ran the War Department telegraph office and saw Lincoln almost daily, asked him about it. Lincoln said he had heard the story before, that it would be very good if he had said it but he did not, and that it was probably charged to him to give it currency. Eckert’s account was published in 1882 Wikiquote, disputed ↗.

Lincoln also identified the ancestor: complaints that General Wolfe was mad drew the royal reply, ‘Well, I wish he would bite some of my other Generals then.’ That he knew the story beforehand is independently corroborated — Admiral Dahlgren’s memoir records Lincoln using it in May 1862, more than a year before the whiskey version appeared the chain ↗.
source.excerptNote: Lincoln’s reply when asked directly, as recorded by Eckert. It is unusual to have a subject on the record denying a quotation attributed to him — and rarer still for him to supply the original.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Lincoln
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln was a famously good storyteller, which is exactly why so many stories became his. Wit attributed to Lincoln gains authority and loses its need for a source. He was aware of the mechanism in his own lifetime — when asked about this very anecdote, he supposed it had been charged to him precisely in order to give it currency.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Very few misattributions can be answered with the subject’s own denial. This one can — and Lincoln went further, identifying the older story the joke had been lifted from.

items.why: Asked directly by a man who saw him daily, Lincoln said he had heard it, that it would be very good if he had said it but he did not, and that it was probably attributed to him to give it currency the denial ↗.

Lincoln named it himself: told Wolfe was mad, the king replied that he wished Wolfe would bite his other generals. Dahlgren’s memoir shows Lincoln using that story in May 1862 — before the whiskey version existed.

items.who: ‘Tell me what brand of whiskey Grant drinks’
items.why: The form most often quoted today has no nineteenth-century printing at all, and the later detail naming a specific brand has no evidence whatsoever. A denied anecdote has kept accreting details for 160 years.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Lincoln — he denied it and named the older King George story behind it. The anecdote first appeared anonymously in the New York Herald on 18 September 1863 full trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a perfect political anecdote: the president defends the general who wins over the generals who complain, and does it with a joke rather than an argument. That it is denied has never slowed it down.

The underlying fact is true, which is why the story sticks. Lincoln did back Grant against his critics — but he did it in writing, plainly, after Vicksburg: ‘I now wish to make the personal acknowledgment that you were right, and I was wrong.’
detailsBody: May 1862: Dahlgren records Lincoln telling the King George / Wolfe story about another general.
13 July 1863: Lincoln writes to Grant after Vicksburg — ‘you were right, and I was wrong.’
18 September 1863: the whiskey anecdote appears anonymously in the New York Herald.
1882: Eckert’s account of Lincoln’s denial is published.
Later: a 19th-century theory crediting the joke to a humourist’s 1864 book does not fit — the newspaper printing predates it by a year.
context.pull: "It would be very good if he had said it, but he did not." — Lincoln, on this quote.
